Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which award did Jean-René Roy receive?
Document 1: **Renowned Canadian Astronomer Honored with Prestigious Knight of the National Order of Quebec**

Montreal, Quebec - In a ceremony held at the Quebec National Assembly, Canadian astronomer Jean-René Roy was bestowed the esteemed title of Knight of the National Order of Quebec, the highest honor conferred by the province. This prestigious recognition acknowledges Roy's outstanding contributions to the field of astronomy and his dedication to promoting scientific literacy in Canada. The National Order of Quebec, established in 1984, is the highest distinction awarded by the Quebec government to individuals who have made significant contributions to the province's cultural, scientific, and social development. The Knight rank, the first of three levels, is reserved for those who have demonstrated exceptional achievements and commitment to their field. Jean-René Roy, a respected figure in the Canadian astronomical community, has spent decades studying the universe and sharing his passion with the public. His groundbreaking research on star formation and galaxy evolution has earned him international recognition, with numerous publications in esteemed scientific journals. "Jean-René Roy is an exceptional scientist and a true ambassador for Canadian astronomy," said Dr. Victoria Kaspi, Director of the McGill Space Institute. "His tireless efforts to promote science education and outreach have inspired countless students and enthusiasts across the country. This honor is a well-deserved recognition of his remarkable achievements." Roy's commitment to science communication has been instrumental in making astronomy accessible to a broader audience. He has written several popular science books, hosted television documentaries, and developed educational programs for schools and museums. "Jean-René Roy's work has not only advanced our understanding of the universe but has also inspired a new generation of scientists and science enthusiasts," said Quebec Minister of Culture and Communications, Nathalie Roy. "His dedication to promoting scientific literacy and critical thinking is a testament to his exceptional character and commitment to the betterment of our society." According to the National Order of Quebec's official website, Roy's induction into the Order is a testament to his "outstanding contributions to the development of astronomy in Quebec and Canada, as well as his commitment to promoting science education and outreach." Data from the National Order of Quebec reveals that since its inception, only a select few have been awarded the Knight rank, making Roy's achievement all the more remarkable. In a statement, Roy expressed his gratitude for the honor, saying, "I am humbled and grateful to receive this prestigious recognition. I hope that this award will inspire others to pursue careers in science and to share their passion with the world."
Document 2: Jean-René Roy

Jean-René Roy is a Canadian astronomer renowned for his groundbreaking research in the field of astrophysics. Born on February 12, 1965, in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, Roy has made significant contributions to the understanding of celestial bodies and their behavior. Early Life and Education

Roy pursued his undergraduate degree in physics from McGill University, graduating magna cum laude in 1987. He then went on to earn his Ph.D. in astronomy from the University of Toronto in 1992, under the supervision of Dr. John Smith. Career

Roy's research focuses on the study of binary star systems and their applications in understanding the universe. He has published numerous papers in esteemed scientific journals, including the Astrophysical Journal and the Astronomical Journal. Awards and Honors

In 1995, Roy was awarded the prestigious Fulbright Scholarship, a highly competitive American educational grant program. This recognition enabled him to conduct research at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, where he collaborated with prominent astronomers and expanded his knowledge in the field. Studies and Research

During his Fulbright tenure, Roy conducted a comprehensive study on the orbital dynamics of binary star systems. His research, published in the journal Science in 1997, provided new insights into the stability of these systems and their potential applications in astrophysical research. In 2001, Roy was part of an international team that discovered a new binary star system, which was later named "Roy's Binary" in his honor. This discovery was published in the journal Nature and garnered significant attention in the scientific community. References
